newsitem.title: USA: LILCO, Brooklyn Union merger to leave N.Y. state with debt.
newsitem.headline: LILCO, Brooklyn Union merger to leave N.Y. state with debt.

text.p: In a major step out of the quagmire created by the defunct Shoreham nuclear plant, Long Island Lighting Co. and Brooklyn Union Gas Wednesday announced long-awaited details of their planned merger, including the assumption of $3.6 billion in Lilco debt by a New York state agency.
Gov. George Pataki said the deal would lower Long Island electric rates, among the highest in the nation, by more than 20 percent over the next five years.

On Dec. 29, the two companies announced their intention to merge in a stock deal creating a $4 billion electric and gas company serving some 2.2 million customers in the New York City boroughs of Brooklyn, Queens and Staten Island and on Long Island east of the city.

Under the agreement, the state's Long Island Power Authority will buy Lilco's electric transmission and distribution system, the company's share of the upstate Nine Mile Point 2 nuclear plant and other assets by paying cash for stock valued at about $2.5 billion in a holding company being formed by Lilco and Brooklyn Union.
That part of the deal is expected to result in proceeds of $1.7 billion to $1.9 billion for Brooklyn Union and Lilco after payment of taxes and short-term debt.

The power authority will also assume or refinance $3.6 billion of Lilco's $4.5 billion debt, they said. The new holding company, which has not yet been named, will assume the remaining $900 million in debt.

The holding company, which has yet to be named, would include all Brooklyn Union operations and Lilco's natural gas system, non-nuclear electricity-generating assets and other assets, the companies said.

They also said they anticipate that $363 million of the $702 million in Lilco preferred stock expected to be outstanding at the close of the deal will be exchanged for preferred stock in the combined company or a subsidiary. The remaining $339 million will be redeemed by the power authority.
The power authority said it expected to finance the deal through tax-exempt bonds.
The deal also calls for the power authority to hire Lilco and Brooklyn Union to run the electrical operations for 15 years.

"This agreement delivers exactly what we need to cut the outrageously expensive electric bills that Long Islanders have been forced to pay for too long," Pataki, who had promised lower rates for Long Islanders, said in a statement.

One of Lilco's biggest and costliest headaches for decades has been its Shoreham nuclear plant in eastern Long Island, which stirred major opposition and never opened. As part of the deal announced Wednesday, the power authority will settle a lawsuit by Lilco alleging that it was overcharged in property taxes by various governments.

The companies said that under the agreement, Lilco shareholders will now get .880 share in the new company for each Lilco share, an increase from the previous ratio of .803 -- giving them a 68 percent piece of the combined company instead of the previously announced 66 percent slice.

The deal is subject to approval by the New York State Public Service Commission, the state's utility regulator board; the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, the Nuclear Regulatory Commission and the Securities and Exchange Commission.
Lilco is based in Hicksville, N.Y. Brooklyn Union's headquarters is in New York City.
The Long Island Power Authority was formed in 1987 to determine whether it was feasible for a public agency to provide power to Long Island instead of Lilco.
